item.title: NWS: Champi expected to pass over or near Guam Sunday morning as a Cat 2 or 3 typhoon
item.description: Emergency officials are warning residents of Guam and Rota to make “the full effort of preparing for a typhoon strike,” as Tropical Storm Champi approaches and continues to intensify. As of the 1 p.m. forecast, Champi was expected to pass over northern Guam as a Category 2 or 3 typhoon on Sunday morning.
item.content:encoded:
Emergency officials are warning residents of Guam and Rota to make “the full effort of preparing for a typhoon strike,” as Tropical Storm Champi approaches and continues to intensify.

As of the 1 p.m. forecast, Champi was expected to pass over northern Guam as a Category 2 or 3 typhoon on Sunday morning.

“This is not a very good outlook for Guam,” Landon Aydlett of the National Weather Service said during a media briefing Friday. Beyond the regular efforts of removing tents, canopies and tarps, Aydlett is advising people to use typhoon shutters and solidify emergency plans.

“Use the next 48 hours wisely,” he said. “Take action, plan, prepare, secure things, secure your homes, and make sure your family has a plan. If you need to be in safe shelter, find that safe shelter. Whether it's an evacuation shelter or with family and friends, make sure you're in a reinforced concrete home or building.”

Although fair weather is expected Saturday morning, conditions will begin deteriorating as the day goes on, Aydlett said.

At 1 p.m. Friday, Tropical Storm Champi was at 11.3 east latitude and 154.0 east longitude, or 590 miles east-southeast of Guam, and moving west at 24 mph.

Guam and Rota were placed under a typhoon warning, with typhoon-force winds of 74 mph or greater expected by Sunday morning.

A typhoon watch was in place for Saipan and Tinian. A flood watch was in effect for all four islands.

Guam Gov. Lou Leon Guerrero placed the island under Condition of Readiness 2.

“I urge everyone to take the necessary precautions and remain attentive to official emergency guidance,” she said. “Our island has faced powerful storms before, and we know that protecting our community requires all of us to do our part. I ask everyone to remain vigilant, look out for their neighbors, and follow the guidance of our emergency officials.”

item.title: Health Professional Licensing Office temporary closure Tuesday
item.description: The Department of Public Health and Social Services will temporarily close its Health Professional Licensing Office from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday. The closure will allow staff to facilitate the National Nurse Aide Assessment Program examinations, which are part of the certification process for individuals seeking to become Certified Nursing Assistants.
item.content:encoded:
The Department of Public Health and Social Services will temporarily close its Health Professional Licensing Office from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday.

The closure will allow staff to facilitate the National Nurse Aide Assessment Program examinations, which are part of the certification process for individuals seeking to become Certified Nursing Assistants.

HPLO services will be unavailable to the public during the closure. Regular office operations will resume at 8 a.m. Wednesday.

For more information, contact HPLO at hplo@dphss.guam.gov or visit guamhplo.org

item.title: Tropical Storm Champi track shifts to the south, passing over Guam
item.description: Tropical Storm Champi’s path has shifted to the south, with the current forecast track taking the storm directly over Guam. However, forecasters caution that the track could still shift.
item.content:encoded:
Tropical Storm Champi’s path has shifted to the south, with the current forecast track taking the storm directly over Guam.

However, forecasters caution that the track could still shift.

Champi is expected to intensify, likely becoming a Category 2 typhoon with winds over 100 mph when it passes through the Marianas this weekend.

As of 4 a.m. Friday, Champi was located at 11.6 degrees north latitude and 156.5 degrees east longitude, or about 800 miles east of Guam. The storm had winds of 40 mph, and it was headed west at 12 mph.

Guam, Rota, Tinian and Saipan are under a typhoon watch and a flood watch. Forecasters say damaging winds are likely late Saturday night and Sunday.

Residents are advised to pick up loose debris on their property, restock their emergency kits and gather any medications or other essentials in preparation for power outages.

item.title: The new Elizabeth Holmes film blends fact, fiction and fraud
item.description: You Can See Everything , the new documentary(-ish?) film about convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes, is best treated as two movies stitched together. item.content:encoded:
You Can See Everything , the new documentary(-ish?) film about convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes, is best treated as two movies stitched together. The first 90 minutes or so, filmed before she went to prison, are a relatively straightforward chronicle of filmmaker Nathan Fielder and his collaborator Lance Oppenheim documenting Holmes' last month at home with her partner, Billy Evans, and their kids. The other 90 minutes are far more experimental, as the story picks up two years later without Holmes available to film. Fielder and Oppenheim have treated their approach to that part of the story as secret; I will not spoil it.

Substantively, the film makes a much better impression as a blend of reality and invention — and not only in the ways it announces itself to be — than it does as a true documentary. If you don't expect to be able to square it with the widely reported facts about its subject, then You Can See Everything is compelling and fascinating, and it contains moments of real insight. (The best one, believe it or not, involves scrambled eggs.) Perhaps ironically, given its title, the best way to enjoy the film is not to look too closely.

That's going to be tough for people who, like me, are Theranos completists . There is a tremendous amount of reporting and investigating that has been done about Theranos, and about Elizabeth Holmes specifically. Still, Fielder, who develops a close bond with Holmes over the course of the film, seemingly chooses to trust his gut and his own conversations with her over all else, and he develops a sort of chin-stroking inability to decide what to think about what she did. He also has an understandable suspicion that she might be trying to play him, at least early on. This is familiar territory for people who encounter her: Even in Alex Gibney's excellent 2019 documentary The Inventor , the question of Holmes' intent vexes some people. Did she convince herself that a sort of "fake it till you make it" approach wasn't exactly lying? Was she so able to fool other people that she fooled herself as well?

You Can See Everything presents some of these same questions, but it stacks the deck in answering them by setting aside some of the evidence that would seem, at the very least, to shed some light. For instance, when Holmes tells Fielder she never lies — never has lied in her life — he is skeptical, but he responds by asking her about things like white lies. Surely, she has told a white lie now and then? Gotten out of a social obligation by pretending to be sick? No? She seems open to the possibility she might have, in those very limited situations, but certainly never, ever about anything of any significance.

As he works through what to make of this claim on her part, Fielder wonders whether she might, in fact, not have lied to her investors as such. For instance, he wonders if a misunderstanding over the word "can" might exonerate her, and whether the rah-rah statements she made about the capabilities of her technology were therefore not intentionally false. Maybe, he wonders, she was just using the word "can" one way and her investors heard it a different way. Maybe it's because, as Billy says, she thinks differently. (I should be clear here that these are things that "Nathan Fielder" the on-screen character wonders. Whether the filmmaker Nathan Fielder, inside his own mind, actually wonders about these things is impossible to know, as is the distance between those two Fielders.)

The problem with spending so much time on this narrow question of what "can" means is that this is not, by any stretch of the imagination, the only thing, or the only kind of thing, that Elizabeth Holmes was accused of lying about. For example, at her trial, Holmes was accused of falsely claiming that her technology was being used by the military on the battlefield , a statement that doesn't lend itself nearly so easily to a linguistic "it depends on your definition of 'can'"-type analysis. But at least in the final cut, Fielder doesn't ask about these other, more concrete untruths and how they might complicate her wide-eyed insistence that she never lies on purpose.

Similarly, when poring over whether Holmes has any malicious intent or is just misunderstood because she's overly literal (and, the film strongly implies but does not quite say, neurodivergent), he never asks her about the whistleblowers who said she tried to ruin their lives with threats, lawyers and private investigators. That, if true, would lend some credence to the idea that she knew she had plenty to hide, rather than having innocently given investors the wrong idea. That consciousness of guilt seems to be precisely the matter at hand. Why not ask her about it?

This selective attention and inattention extends even to what happens between the subjects and the filmmakers. Fielder becomes fixated at one point, as communication with Evans breaks down, on the terms of the agreement between the couple and A24 — and whether they would profit from the film. Fielder wonders what Holmes knows of the financial negotiation, and what Evans may (or may not) have shared with her. But ... presumably, Fielder has access to whatever paperwork they signed, since it's his movie. The obvious question is: What, if anything, did Holmes sign, and what did it say? There are suggestions she might not have needed to sign anything at all, but it feels murkier than it should. When Fielder the on-screen character doesn't reckon with evidence that it seems like Fielder the filmmaker should have — and doesn't explain why not — the uncomfortable sense that there's some willful sleight-of-hand going on creeps in. (And again, some varieties of sleight-of-hand with reenactments and such are well within Fielder's usual box of tricks; this is different, particularly if he's not transparent about whether he's doing it.)

Fielder aficionados, of whom there are many, will tell you enthusiastically that this bafflement is the point of his methods and of his style. He wants you to find it all very trippy, to question what's real and what's not. He wants you to wonder what to think, including about him. That's true, and he's very good at it, and it works exceptionally well when the ambiguity originates in the messy nature of a real situation and in the strange nature of human behavior, as it does in the film's treatment of some of the underlying dynamics of Holmes and Evans' relationship. It feels a bit more hollow and more manipulative if questions are artificially rendered unanswerable through the setting aside of available evidence.

If you treat You Can See Everything as a kind of fact-fiction blend, which it more glaringly becomes in its second half, it is an enormously skilled piece of filmmaking that pulls on precisely the threads it means to. It creates a grayer-than-gray version of Elizabeth Holmes who credibly might, in fact, mostly be a victim of a lot of misunderstandings and some bad relationship choices. Seeing Fielder wrestle with that possibility — particularly as someone who touched, during the second season of The Rehearsal , on his own ambivalence about potentially being diagnosed as neurodivergent — is genuinely gripping. It's even touching, maybe.

But if you read John Carreyrou's Bad Blood , and if you listen to the accompanying podcast, and if you watch The Inventor , and if you read about what unfolded at her fraud trial, it's fair to wonder whether You Can See Everything 's version of Elizabeth Holmes is, at its heart, a creation of the filmmakers that could do a disservice to people who treat it as real, as well as to the people who suffered real consequences from her actions. Not just the Theranos investors, but regular people who said they got incorrect test results from Theranos machines, and those whistleblowers, and other people who worked for her and were sucked into her orbit.

Fielder and Oppenheim's "Liz" is assembled at least in part through the clever use of narrative negative space — through leaving in what supports this "it's complicated, who knows?" version of her and leaving out whatever suggests that in reality, that might be a lot of hooey, and she might not be all that different from anybody else who commits a large-scale fraud. That a leader did not initially set out to rip anybody off doesn't mean there was no dishonesty. Even the co-creator of the Fyre Festival , who was also convicted of fraud , may have hoped it would be a big success when the planning started. He, too, was probably sad about going to prison.

"It's not that deep" is not much of a three-hour documentary logline, and it wouldn't make a movie nearly as interesting as this one. But what if that, in fact, is the truth?

item.title: Amid talk of public execution, public opinion on death penalty is split
item.description: U.S. public sentiment about the death penalty has come to the forefront after President Trump gave his blessing, then backtracked, to livestreaming an execution via firing squad . That planned execution comes after two botched Tennessee lethal injections this year , where the state struggled to find veins to administer death-inducing drugs to Christa Pike and Tony Carruthers.
item.content:encoded:
U.S. public sentiment about the death penalty has come to the forefront after President Trump gave his blessing, then backtracked, to livestreaming an execution via firing squad .

That planned execution comes after two botched Tennessee lethal injections this year , where the state struggled to find veins to administer death-inducing drugs to Christa Pike and Tony Carruthers.

Speaking at a press conference a day after Pike's failed execution, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said Tennesseans were disappointed about what happened.

"The people of Tennessee have determined that the death penalty is an appropriate penalty for the most heinous crimes in this state," he said. "The people of Tennessee make that decision and my job is to make sure that those sentences are carried out."

Those Tennesseans join some two-thirds of Americans who support the death penalty for people convicted of murder, according to a Pew Research Center poll from this summer . According to PRRI, a nonpartisan nonprofit , people that favor the punishment tend to be Christian, white and vote Republican.

Daniel LaChance, a history professor at Emory University, says the overall numbers mask a wide range of opinions.

" Support for the death penalty in the United States is a mile wide and an inch deep," says LaChance, who also wrote the book "Executing Freedom: The Cultural Life of Capital Punishment in the United States."

That's because the polling is incredibly nuanced, LaChance said. When polls offer more variance in the questions, such as life without parole, 60% of Americans support that over the death penalty. The number drops even further when monetary support to the victims' family members is an option.

And separate 2025 polling from Gallup — which has been tracking support for the death penalty since 1937 — shows that 52% of Americans support the death penalty if a person is convicted of murder, the lowest share in more than 50 years.

The Death Penalty Information Center, a nonprofit that tracks the use of the death penalty but does not take a position on it, has counted 203 people since 1972 who were exonerated after being wrongfully convicted and sentenced to death.

"Those are just the ones we know about," says Robin Maher, the nonprofit's executive director. "We don't know how many innocent people were executed before we learned about their claims."

The wrongful death sentences, plus the moral efficacy, are what is swaying the public's opinion, Maher said.

"For the public to realize that the death penalty system was fallible, that it made serious mistakes, raised a lot of issues in people's minds about whether this very costly public policy, that was nonetheless rather inaccurate and unfair, should be used," Maher said.

The Pew Research Center study from July also found that while most people support the death penalty for crimes like murder, some 59% of respondents in the survey said the death penalty does not deter people from committing serious crimes – versus 39% who believe it does.

Six states were responsible for the 31 executions in 2026 — even though 27 states still legally allow the most severe form of punishment in this country. Florida led the way, with more than half of the executions this year.

Maher says that the fact that more than half the states allow capital punishment, but are issuing fewer death sentences, shows that the American people are disenchanted with the use of the death penalty.

" More often than not, they are finding it is not the right answer to violent crime," she says. "Executions on the other hand, are the result of what a handful of elected officials in just a few states are doing."

Texas accounts for the most executions since the 1970s, while Michigan holds the title for the longest-running death penalty abolition in the U.S., after banning the practice in 1847.

The planned execution by firing squad is of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist stationed at Fort Hood, Texas, who killed 13 people and wounded 32 in 2009. It's slated for December but appeals could delay it further.

While 52% of Americans support Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan's execution, 80% say his death should not be livestreamed , according to an October poll from ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos.

When Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced earlier this month that Hasan would be executed publicly, the U.S. also hadn't conducted a high-profile public execution in 90 years.

In certain parts of America, quasi-public executions drew up to 10,000 viewers in the past, said LaChance, the Emory history professor. But the growing use of medicine such as anesthesia began a negative shift in public executions.

" Pain, especially in public spaces, starts to seem scandalous," LaChance says. "It's preventable now. It starts to seem barbaric."

LaChance also said the public, especially in immigrant communities, would turn the executed into heroes. "They would claim the body and conduct little parades in Lower Manhattan, celebrating the life of the person who had been put to death," he said.

One U.S. official who spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity out of fear of retribution said President Trump was talked out of a livestream execution because it was against American values — but also because there was concern the tape would show up on Jihadi websites, leading to an increase in recruits and possible danger to U.S. forces in the Middle East.

" That's the story of the death penalty," LaChance says. "People didn't want public executions to disappear when they did. Elites did because they were becoming embarrassing carnivals."

item.title: Israeli settlers beat Palestinians and a U.S. photojournalist in West Bank attacks
item.description: Updated October 17, 2026 at 2:58 AM ChST Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians as they were harvesting olives in the occupied West Bank on Friday, injuring several people including an American photojournalist.
item.content:encoded:
Updated October 17, 2026 at 2:58 AM ChST

Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians as they were harvesting olives in the occupied West Bank on Friday, injuring several people including an American photojournalist.

The Washington Post said photographer Heidi Levine was reporting in the West Bank, wearing a protective vest clearly marked as "press," when she was beaten.

"Today I was brutally attacked," Levine said in a video filmed at a hospital. "We saw in the distance, in the hilltop, I would say at least 50 masked men, slingshots. And when they came running down, I was attacked, pushed to the ground." She said "they just kept kicking me and kicking me." They also tore her cameras and phone off her.

She said medical workers rushed her in an ambulance to a hospital. Washington Post Executive Editor Matt Murray said in a statement Levine has received medical care and is safe.

"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," Murray said.

Israeli police issued a statement acknowledging reports that a foreign journalist was injured and said it would investigate the incident and "bring those involved to justice."

The U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem said it was aware and monitoring the situation. Without mentioning Levine's attack specifically, it said in a statement, "We are in regular dialogue with partners about improving stability and security in the West Bank. We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests, and convictions, of those responsible."

The Washington Post said the attack happened when Palestinians were trying to gather their olive harvest. It said settlers set Palestinian olive groves on fire and hurled stones using slingshots.

There were two dozen settler attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters Friday, leaving 20 people injured, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent Society.

The attacks came as groups of Israeli settlers have stepped up their assaults on Palestinians in the West Bank. They also follow another attack earlier this month, when Israelis beat Agence France-Presse photojournalist Jaafar Ashtiyeh , as he was covering settler violence against Palestinian olive farmers in the West Bank.

Sara Qudah of the Committee to Protect Journalists said Levine's beating was not an isolated incident for journalists covering the West Bank olive harvest. "It's part of a disturbing pattern of violence and harassment against journalists regardless of their nationalities," she said. She added that the attackers have no reason to fear consequences because Israeli authorities have failed to stop them.

Palestinian Journalists Syndicate also condemned the attack as an "assault on press freedom" and violation of rules protecting journalists during conflicts.

Nuha Musleh contributed reporting from Ramallah, West Bank.

item.title: Crowds throng New Delhi and wave Indian flags amid escalating protests

item.content:encoded:
NEW DELHI — Thousands of Indians thronged a bustling thoroughfare in the heart of the capital, waving the national flag and demanding the resignation of the country's election chief, the latest show of public dissent against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.

The protesters rallied in Connaught Place, one of New Delhi's busiest commercial districts, responding to a call by the youth "Cockroach" movement, whose leader Abhijeet Dipke was detained by police ahead of the demonstration. Protesters spanning generations joined the rally, reflecting broad public anger and intensifying pressure on the country's top election official.

Protests by the youth and opposition parties have intensified over an ongoing review of voter lists that has removed more than 130 million names since last year. Critics say the exercise is politically motivated, threatens to disenfranchise millions more, and has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims. They have demanded the resignation of election chief Gyanesh Kumar.

The Election Commission and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's administration deny the allegations and say the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries.

Friday's protest was part of a growing campaign that has put Modi's government under pressure and comes a week after a police crackdown on protesters in New Delhi.

The demonstrators vastly outnumbered the security personnel lining the road, while columns of riot police stood watch.

Police had earlier asked people not to join the rally and offered to let a small group gather to wave the national flag and sing the national anthem. In anticipation of the protests, authorities also closed Central Park, a green space surrounded by Connaught Place's white colonial-era buildings, on Friday and Saturday.

Modi has not publicly commented on the protests. Some of his party leaders have dismissed the demonstrators as "anarchists" and suggested, without offering evidence, that they are backed by foreign powers.

Police detained Dipke, the founder of the "Cockroach" movement, ahead of the demonstrations. He had urged supporters unable to travel to New Delhi to raise the flag and demonstrate in their own communities.

A live video posted on the movement's Instagram account showed Dipke leaving a house and heading toward the street, where police officers intercepted him. After a brief exchange, officers hauled him into a police vehicle and drove away.

"Waving the tricolor (Indian flag) is not a crime," he told reporters Thursday.

The "Cockroach" movement began as an online satirical campaign this summer after India's chief justice compared unemployed young people to parasites. Many young Indians embraced the remark, adopting the cockroach as a symbol of resilience. It has since expanded into a nationwide protest movement of young people. Protests led by the group forced the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, a rare setback for the prime minister, who has been in power for more than 12 years.

It remains unclear whether the protests will grow into a wider political movement. Modi's government remains electorally strong, and anger over voter lists may not necessarily translate into support for the opposition, which has used the issue to criticize his Hindu nationalist government.
